list.listitem: Thrombocytopenia (TCP) has many potential causes and can be multifactorial. It is diagnosed based on a platelet count of less than 150,000 platelets/microliter (μL). C
Initial evaluation should include complete blood count (CBC) and peripheral blood smear; consider a platelet antibody (direct) test as well. C

Treatment is not always necessary. The goal is to prevent bleeding and complications and to maintain a safe platelet count, which will vary based on the etiology of the TCP and the clinical scenario. Treat the patient, not the platelet number, unless it is less than 10,000 platelets/μL. C
If possible, stop drugs that may cause TCP (see ). A
Advise hospitalization and consider hematology consultant if the patient has symptoms of bleeding. C
Guidelines for monitoring of heparin-induced TCP (HIT) are shown in . Routine screening for HIT antibodies in the absence of symptoms is not recommended because of the test's lack of specificity. B

background.definition: TCP is defined as a platelet count of less than 150,000/μL. Severe TCP is typically defined as a platelet count of less than 50,000/μL. In late pregnancy, TCP is defined as a platelet count less than 120,000/μL. There are two types of HIT. HIT type I is benign and clinically insignificant. It occurs within a few days of heparin treatment and does not increase bleeding or thrombosis risk. Platelet counts generally do not decrease below 100,000 platelets/μL and increase to normal after several days even with continued heparin use. HIT type I is not discussed further in this chapter. HIT type II will be referred to in this chapter as HIT.

list.listitem: Most studies on the incidence of TCP are in ICU settings, where the range is 19% to 44%.
In the ICU, the incidence of a platelet count of less than 20,000/μL is less than 5%.
The incidence of heparin-induced TCP (HIT) in patients exposed to heparin is 0.2% to 0.39%.
Consider reasonable activity, sports, and occupational restrictions based on the degree of TCP.
See for causes of TCP.

A systematic review of randomized controlled trials found no difference in the risk of HIT between low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) and unfractionated heparin (UFH) (1.2% for enoxaparin, 1.5% for UFH).

There are four main pathophysiological mechanisms of TCP: decreased production, increased destruction, splenic sequestration, and loss of platelets (see ). TCP can be multifactorial. Decreased production: marrow failure or marrow replacement. Increased destruction or consumption: autoantibodies to platelet antigens, mechanical destruction as in cardiac bypass patients. Increased splenic sequestration: from hypersplenism, which increases the spleen's filtering and destruction of platelets. Loss of platelets: resulting from hemorrhage.

list.listitem: ITP is a clinical diagnosis based on the exclusion of other causes of TCP. The history, physical, CBC, and peripheral smear should show only TCP and no other abnormalities. Serologic confirmation with antiplatelet antibodies is not necessary.

HIT type II is a clinical and serologic diagnosis. HIT antibody formation is found in conjunction with an unexplained platelet count decline (90% of patients will have a count of more than 50% of baseline, even if nadir platelet is more than 150,000/μL) during heparin treatment. Alternatively, it may be also diagnosed by acute systemic reactions (cardiorespiratory distress, acute inflammatory reactions, or other such signs) within 30 minutes of intravenous (IV) UFH or the presence of skin lesions at the site of heparin injection.

TCP can be asymptomatic and is often detected incidentally. Bleeding is uncommon with a platelet count between 50,000 and 100,000/μL but occurs frequently in patients with a platelet count between 10,000 and 50,000/μL. Patients with a platelet count less than 10,000/μL can have severe, spontaneous hemorrhage.

Look for bleeding complications resulting from TCP. In the ICU, the bleeding rate was 4.1% for platelets more than 150,000/μL, 21.4% for platelets 101-149,000/μL, and 52.6% for platelets less than 100,000/μL (odds ratio [OR] 4.0, 95% CI = 1.8-8.9, P = .0005).
Most common sites of bleeding in ICU patients with TCP are gastrointestinal (39.3%), ENT/airways (29.5%), and puncture site (27.9%). In 19.7%, there was more than one site of bleeding.
Bleeding may also occur in the urinary system or cause menorrhagia in females, or petechiae, purpura, or ecchymoses may be noted.
Venous thrombosis may be present in DIC and HIT. In addition, arterial thrombosis may also be found in HIT.
TCP may be found in splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly if hypersplenism exists.
Inquire about medications that can cause TCP ().
Initial evaluation should include CBC and peripheral blood smear.

To distinguish immune from nonimmune causes of TCP, consider a platelet antibody (direct) done by flow cytometry to detect platelet-associated IgGs or by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to detect glycoprotein-specific platelet antibodies. A positive result indicates the presence of antibodies bound to the platelet surface.

An indirect platelet antibody will be positive in neonatal alloimmune TCP or posttransfusion purpura. This is done by enzyme immunassay, and a positive result indicates the presence of circulating antibodies to platelet-specific and/or HLA-class antigens. It can have false negatives.
See chapter on immune thrombocytopenia purpura. Elevated plasma thrombopoietin and at least 2% reticulated platelets support this diagnosis.

If clinical scenario is highly suspicious for HIT, consider checking a heparin-induced platelet antibody (antiplatelet factor 4 antibody). Use this test to rule out HIT rather than to confirm the diagnosis because it has a high negative predictive value but only a moderate positive predictive value. This is a sensitive (90%-98%) but not completely specific (71%) test for HIT because not all anti-platelet factor 4 (PF4) antibodies are clinically significant. This is a PF4-dependent ELISA.

The serotonin release assay is considered the "gold standard" for the diagnosis of HIT but is not widely available. This is a platelet activation assay with higher sensitivity and specificity for detecting the clinically relevant antibodies compared with the heparin-induced platelet antibody.
If abnormalities are found in other cell lines (white or red blood cells), consider a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.

Consider testing for and treating Helicobacter pylori in patients who appear to have chronic ITP. H. pylori may contribute to the pathogenesis of chronic ITP through a molecular similarity between platelets and H. pylori antigens. The prevalence of H. pylori infection in chronic ITP is approximately 63%, compared with approximately 30% in the general US population.
See for a suggested approach to the initial evaluation and management of TCP.
Transfuse if platelets are less than 10,000/μL, even if asymptomatic, because there is a significant risk of serious spontaneous bleeding. C
Corticosteroids are usually the first-line treatment for TCP caused by ITP. C
Thrombopoietin agonists like eltrombopag and romiplostim are increasingly used for immune thrombocytopenia.B
Corticosteroids are usually the first-line treatment for TCP caused by ITP.
Remember to discontinue drugs that may be causing TCP, if possible ().

A large meta-analysis showed that standard treatment for H. pylori in patients with ITP shows a statistically significant increase in platelet counts compared with those untreated, unsuccessfully treated, or without H. pylori. A small study showed that the platelet count was then successfully maintained over a mean follow-up time of 25.8 months.
Romiplostim, a thrombopoietin mimetic that increases platelet production, is a safe, effective (and expensive!) treatment to raise platelet counts and avoid splenectomy in patients with ITP.

In children with newly diagnosed primary immune thrombocytopenia, a randomized trial with 71 participants f ound that the thrombopoietin agonist eltrombopag was effective (65% vs 35% response, p = 0.002, NNT = 3).
A splenectomy may be indicated for TCP caused by ITP.

Platelet transfusion is not always indicated in TCP, and it is contraindicated in TTP (unless there is a life-threatening hemorrhage) and heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), because it may worsen the clinical scenario.

Treat the patient, not the platelet count number, unless it is less than 10,000/μL. Transfuse if the platelet count is less than 10,000/μL, even if asymptomatic, because there is a significant risk of serious, spontaneous bleeding.

When a platelet transfusion is indicated, it is recommended to give one adult dose over 30 minutes, which should increase the platelet level by at least 20,000/μL. In a child weighing less than 20 kg, use 10 to 15 mL/kg up to the adult dose and transfuse at a rate of 20 to 30 mL/(kg h). The optimal dose and frequency of transfusion vary based on the individual clinical scenario.

The response to a platelet transfusion can be assessed by the clinical response if the patient was actively bleeding. In the outpatient setting, a platelet count can be obtained 10 minutes after the transfusion; this gives a result identical to results checked more than 1 hour after the transfusion.
Risks of transfusion are: alloimmunization, infection, allergic reaction, and transfusion-related acute lung injury.

Platelet transfusion decreases catheter-related bleeding compared to no-transfusion during ultrasound guided catheter placement in patients with platelet levels 10,000 to 50,000 per cubic millimeter (NNT = 14).
Advise hospitalization and consider hematology consultant if the patient has symptoms of bleeding.

In late pregnancy, TCP is defined as a platelet count of less than 120,000/μL.
In preterm infants with thrombocytopenia, transfusion at a lower threshold (25,000) improves outcomes compared to a higher threshold (50,000).

list.listitem: For patients receiving heparin who are at a rare risk (<0.1%) of developing HIT, it is recommended not to monitor platelet counts routinely. Rare risk is defined as medical/obstetrical patients receiving LMWH or medical patients receiving unfractionated heparins (UFHs) catheter flushes.
For all other patients receiving heparin who are at a >0.1% risk of developing HIT, monitoring platelet counts is recommended over not monitoring platelet counts.

Obtain a baseline platelet count and a repeat count in 24 h in any patient who received, or may have received or in whom exposure is uncertain, UFH in the past 100 days and who is going to receive UFH or LMWH.
Monitor platelets counts at least every other day until day 14 or UFH is discontinued, whichever happens first, for patients receiving therapeutic doses of UFH.

Monitor platelet counts at least every other day between postoperative days 4 and 14, or until UFH is discontinued, whichever happens first, for patients receiving UFH for postoperative antithrombotic prophylaxis.

Monitor platelet counts every 2 to 3 days from day 4 to day 14, or until heparin is discontinued, whichever happens first, for patients receiving prophylactic-dose UFH, postoperative patients receiving prophylactic-dose LMWH or intravascular catheter UFH flushes, and patients receiving LMWH after first receiving UFH.
Monitor platelet count immediately in any patient with any acute symptoms within 30 min of an IV UFH bolus.
